Fear-setting is Tim Ferriss's written exercise for a decision that has stalled
on fear rather than on information. It descends from the Stoic practice of
rehearsing the bad outcome in advance, and Seneca's line that we suffer more
often in imagination than in reality is the claim it tests. The exercise is done
on paper, as three pages, because a fear held in the head stays vague and a fear
written out turns out to be smaller and more answerable.

## The Three Pages

1. **"What if I…?"** Name the action being avoided, then fill three columns.
   **Define**: the worst things that could follow, listed to exhaustion rather
   than to ten. **Prevent**: what would reduce the chance of each one.
   **Repair**: what you would do if it happened anyway, and who you would ask.
2. **The benefits of an attempt, or of partial success.** What a version that
   only half works still buys you.
3. **The cost of inaction.** What not acting costs at six months, one year and
   three years, priced separately in money, in health and in how it feels. This
   page is the one that usually decides it, because the cost of doing nothing
   accrues quietly while the cost of acting is the only one being imagined.

## Why It Works on a Page

A feared outcome with a repair written next to it stops being a reason not to
act. Most entries in the Define column turn out to be recoverable in a sentence,
and the few that are not are the ones deserving the attention the whole list was
absorbing.
